en: The Jātaka of the Forty:
The Section on the Tesakuṇa Birds.
4. The Saṅkhapāla Jātaka:
“You have the appearance of one who is noble, with eyes full of serene faith;
I think, sir, that you have gone forth from a family of high standing.”
“How indeed, O god among men, did the wise one, having abandoned wealth and enjoyments,
go forth from his home?
“Having seen his own celestial mansion, O god among men,”
"O King, having seen the great fruit of merit of the majestic Mahoraga,
I have gone forth out of faith."
“Neither out of desire for sensual pleasures, nor out of fear,
nor out of hatred do those who have gone forth speak a word of falsehood.
Being asked about this matter, tell it to me.”
“Having heard this, faith was born within me.
“O Lord of the Realm, while traveling on my business,
I saw the son of a Bhoja woman on the road.”
As they went along, delighted, carrying a great snake with its body extended, I,
O Lord of Men, approached them.
With my hair standing on end, I was terrified and cried out:
"Where is this one of fearsome body being led?
What will you do with him, O sons of Bhoja?"
“‘This nāga is being led away for the sake of food—
a great serpent with a massive body;
its flesh is savory, abundant, and tender.’”
"You do not know taste, son of Videha.
Having gone from here to our own home,
we shall take up our weapons and do violence."
“Delighting in eating their flesh,
we shall indeed become the food of the serpents.
“If this one is being led away for the sake of food...”
"A great serpent with a body fully grown;
I give you sixteen oxen—
release this nāga from his bonds!"
"Truly, this food of ours is pleasing,
and many snakes have been eaten by us before;
we shall do as you say, Āḷāra."
"And be moderate with us, O son of Videha.
Then they indeed released him from his bonds,
from that snare which had been set for him.
That Naga king, released from his bonds,
set out facing the east for a moment;
having gone facing the east for a moment, he departed.
He looked at me with eyes full of joy;
then I followed behind him,
raising my ten-fingered hands in reverent salutation.
“You should indeed go with all haste,
lest your enemies seize you again;
for reunion with hunters is painful.”
"Go, sir, to where the Bhojaputtas cannot see you.
He went to a lake that was perfectly clear,
blue-lustrous, delightful, and with beautiful bathing-places.
Covered with rose-apple trees and reeds,
he crossed over, his fear dispelled and his mind at peace.
Having entered it, before long that elephant—
By means of my divine power, O Lord of Men, you appeared before me;
you attended upon me like a son to his father,
speaking words that were heart-stirring and pleasant to the ear.
“You are my mother and father, Āḷāra;
you are my inner life-giver and friend.
And I am one who has obtained his own supernormal power.”
Behold my dwellings, Āḷāra;
they abound in food and have plenty of grain and drink,
like Masakkasāra belongs to Vāsava.
That ground, endowed with excellent features,
was free of pebbles, soft, and beautiful;
the earth had low-growing grass and little dust.
Where the serene abandon their sorrow—
there is a most delightful mango grove, not crowded, as blue as beryl, extending in all four directions.
"Ripe and unripe fruits are fully blossomed;
though their stalks are withered, they still bear fruit.
O god among men, in the midst of those forests...
The dwelling, with a radiance like the morning sun,
with silver thresholds and made of gold,
magnificent, shines like lightning in the sky.
Exquisite, made of jewels and gold,
manifold and ever-well-fashioned,
they are filled with adorned maidens.
Wearing golden armlets, O King,
that Saṅkhapāla of extraordinary beauty ascended the palace with great haste.
A palace with a thousand pillars and incomparable majesty,
where his chief queen resided;
and one woman, hurrying with all speed—
Taking up a precious, costly beryl gem,
beautiful and possessed of natural excellence,
she approached the seat without being prompted.
Then the serpent took me by the hand and seated me upon a seat facing him, saying:
"May the venerable sir sit here on this seat."
"For you, sir, are one of my elders.
Then another woman,
hurrying along and carrying water, approached.
She washed my feet, O Lord of Men,
like a wife for her own dear husband;
and another woman, moving with great haste, [did the same].
Taking up a golden bowl,
he presented him with food of pleasing appearance, consisting of many soups and various kinds of curries.
O Bhārata, when I had finished eating with the four [kinds of food],
I attended upon my husband, knowing his mind; thereafter,
he fell down before me, great as I was.
"With no small celestial pleasures:
'These three hundred wives of mine, O Āḷāra,
all of middle age and radiant as lotuses;"
“Āḷāra, these are at your disposal;
I give them to you—enjoy them.
Having experienced divine flavors for a year, [he said:]
Then I spoke further to him with kindness:
“What is this, O Naga, and how was it obtained?
How did you come by this most excellent celestial mansion?”
Was this obtained by chance, born of transformation,
made by yourself, or given by the gods?
O King of Nagas, I ask you about this matter.
“How did you come to possess this most excellent celestial mansion?
“It was not obtained by supernatural power, nor born of transformation;
it was not made by myself, nor given by the gods.”
"Through wholesome deeds, through blameless and meritorious actions,
this celestial mansion has been obtained by me.
"What was your vow, and what was your holy life?"
"Of what well-performed deed is this the result?
Tell me this matter, O King of Nagas:
how was this celestial mansion obtained by you?"
“I was once the king of the Magadhans,
a lord of great power named Duyyodhana;
having recognized that life is but brief, [I renounced it].”
It is impermanent and subject to change.
With a confident heart, I gave abundant gifts of food and drink with due respect.
My home was then like a well,
where ascetics and brahmins were satisfied;
with garlands, perfumes, and ointments, [I honored them].
There we gave gifts with due respect: lamps, vehicles, and dwellings; clothing, bedding, as well as food and drink.
That was my vow, and that was my holy life;
this is the fruit of that well-practiced conduct.
By that very merit, I have obtained this celestial mansion.
It has abundant food, much drink,
and is filled with dancing, singing, and other delights;
it endures for a long time, yet it is not eternal.”
“Those of little power destroy one of great power, those lacking splendor destroy the splendid.
Why is this so, O fang-weaponed one? On what does it depend?”
It has come into the hands of beggars.
Has some great fear come upon you,
or has your fiery energy departed from the roots of your teeth?
“O Daṭhāvudha, why, depending on what,
did you commit an offense against the forest-dwelling mendicants?
“No great fear has come upon me.”
They cannot destroy my splendor;
the well-proclaimed teachings of the virtuous are as impossible to overstep as the shore of the ocean.
On the fourteenth and the fifteenth day, Āḷāra,
I always observe the Uposatha;
then the sixteen Bhojaputta youths arrived.
Having taken a strong rope and a snare,
the hunters pierced my nose, passed the rope through it,
and led me away while grasping me all around.
"I endured such suffering,
not violating the Uposatha day.
"They saw you on that path of solitude," they said.
Deprived of strength and beauty,
yet cultivated with glory and wisdom,
what do you aspire to, O Naga, that you perform this asceticism?
“Not for the sake of a son, not for the sake of wealth,
nor even for the sake of long life, O Āḷāra,
but desiring the human state, [I have come].”
"Therefore, exerting myself, I shall practice asceticism.
"You, with blood-red eyes and broad chest,
adorned and with hair and beard trimmed;"
Anointed with red sandalwood,
you illuminate the quarters like the King of the Gandharvas;
you have attained divine power, O one of great majesty.
Endowed with all sensual pleasures,
I ask you this matter, O King of Nagas:
in what way is the world of humans better than this?
‘Āḷāra, purity or self-restraint does not exist anywhere other than in the human world. And I,
having obtained a human birth, [shall practice it].’
"I shall bring an end to birth and death.
"A year has passed for me living in your presence;
I have been served with food and drink."
"Having called out, O Naga, I am fleeing;
I have been away from home for a long time, O Lord of Men.
"Sons, wives, and dependents—"
"Instructed by me constantly, attend to this;
I hope that no one has cursed you,
for I love to see you, Āḷāra."
"Just as a beloved son might live provided for in the home of his mother and father,
even better than that for me is this very place here."
“Indeed, O Naga, your mind is full of faith.
“I possess a ruby, a magnificent jewel that brings wealth.”
"Take this and go to your own home;
having obtained that wealth, you should give up this jewel.
I have seen even human sensual pleasures."
They are impermanent and subject to change;
having seen the peril in the strands of sensual pleasure,
O King, I have gone forth out of faith.
Like ripe fruits falling from trees,
young and old alike fall upon the dissolution of the body;
seeing this too, O King, I have gone forth.
“The ascetic life alone is certainly better.
“Truly, those who are wise,
learned, and thinkers on many matters should indeed be served.”
"Having heard of you and the four Nāgas,
I shall perform no small amount of merit.
"Truly, those endowed with wisdom must certainly be served."
"O King, those who are learned and contemplate many matters—
having heard both the Naga and me—
perform abundant meritorious deeds."
The Saṅkhapāla Jātaka is the fourth.
